extracted.intended_audience: beginner reporters; journalism students; cub reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instruction for beginners in newspaper reporting: how to gather, handle, and write news stories for city desks and metropolitan newspapers. Covers organization of papers, news values, sources, interviewing, leads, story organization, sentence/paragraph/word-level style, specialized story types, and mechanical/production processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: News defined / News values
rubrics_metrics.description: What news is and its values (nose for news): the qualities that make an item newsworthy — unusualness, human interest, record-breaking, life lost, extremes, nearness, interest, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn to know values of news: seek the unusual, the extremes, record-breaking events, heroism, pathos, human interest; assess nearness/localization and personal interest. The reporter must develop a 'nose for news' and know the values so he can recognize and get items into print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in news
rubrics_metrics.description: News must be accurate in facts, names, figures, dates, and assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify facts with witnesses and records; use note-book and shorthand; detect falsehoods; check names, addresses, and spellings; the book repeatedly emphasizes accuracy (index refs: 26, 57, 67, 74, 84, 116, 128, 141, 146).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / Speed
rubrics_metrics.description: News must be timely — brought to the public promptly; speed is a primary journalistic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue scoops and runs; use speed devices (fudge, special telegraph lines, compositors) to get late news into editions; know printing and mechanical limits; prioritize timeliness when appropriate without sacrificing accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization / Nearness of events
rubrics_metrics.description: Localizing stories increases interest — place and proximity matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localize national or distant items when possible; use local angles, local names, and effects to make copy more relevant to the paper's readership (references: localization, near-ness of events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Know, cultivate, and use a variety of news sources — police, courts, hospitals, morgue, exchange, telegraph, correspondents, business and social contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain beats; build relationships with police blotter, state correspondents, morgue/library, exchange editor, market and telegraph editors; keep a space book and string for correspondents; supply and use the morgue for background material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting the story (assignments/beats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for obtaining stories: assignments, beats, interviews, telephoning, following up, and using printed/mailing sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should know how to start for stories, use telephone and telegraph, make appointments, visit scenes, attend hearings, and follow instructions from city editor; keep note-book and practice memory and note-taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Following up / Follow-ups / Rewrites
rubrics_metrics.description: After an initial dispatch, reporters should follow up to develop fuller accounts and subsequent developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow-up stories (slugged 'follow' or 'follow-ups') should add facts, sources, reactions, and continuity; rewrite men prepare fuller accounts for later editions; know how to manage advance copies and release stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of the story (overall structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: How a news story should be organized: lead, body, order (time, space, climactic, complex), unity and coherence of impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate organizational order (summaries, climactic, time, space); keep unity of impression and coherence; arrange paragraphs and sentences to support the lead and the single dominant idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: The lead / lede — selection and wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead is the point of greatest difficulty and requires careful choice and effective wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads should summarize the main point, be clear and interesting; types discussed include summarized leads, question leads, suspense/suspensive leads, informal leads, verse leads, and those for features, speeches, interviews, crimes, accidents, deaths, and sports. Practice constructing good leads; many examples are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the story — development after the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: The body should amplify, explain, and supply details supporting the lead, using orderly presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide important facts early; use paragraphs to group related facts; avoid contradictions and repetitions; retain proportion and emphasis; include quotations and background as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: The paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs have definite laws and should be used to group related ideas; the book treats the paragraph lightly but emphasizes its role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraphs should be coherent units; use indention/paragraph marks properly in copy; avoid shifting subjects within paragraphs; keep paragraphs short for newspaper readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: The sentence — clarity, unity, force
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences must be clear, direct, unified, and forceful; sentence-level craft is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor short, active constructions; avoid ambiguity of pronouns; keep agreement; use correct verb forms; watch coordination/subordination; maintain unity and proportion in sentence elements (chapter on the sentence treats mechanics and style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice / diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words carefully for clearness, precision, brevity, and appropriateness to the paper's tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trite phrases and slang (except in sports when appropriate), prefer common words, avoid vague phrasing; strive for elegance without obscurity; the 'Words' chapter and style book entries give guidance on preferred forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations and interviews — accuracy and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must record and use quotations accurately; interviewing requires skill in questioning and making people talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verbatim quotations when appropriate; prepare questions; use telephone interviews properly; check testimony and motive; know when to paraphrase and when to quote; interview practice and sample questions are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting falsehoods / checking motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter must detect falsehood and understand motives behind statements to assess reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check witness statements, look for inconsistencies, contrast with documentary evidence; use discretion in accepting sensational or self-interested claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of libel and legal caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors must avoid libel and be cautious about publishing defamatory statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy readers, managing editor, and editor-in-chief check for libel; reporters should avoid unverified accusations, secure corroboration, and be aware that proofs are read for possible libel; guidance on pruning libelous statements and editorial checks is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorializing / avoiding bias
rubrics_metrics.description: News copy should avoid editorializing and reflect the paper's editorial policies without inserting reporter's opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctly separate news reporting from editorials; be aware of and adapt to newspaper policies and owner/editor influence; exchange editors and managing editors oversee bias and policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of news / ethical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are occasions and policies regarding suppression of news; reporters must know when suppression is exercised and ethical implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: City editor or managing editor may suppress stories; reporters should follow orders but be mindful of suppression causes (security, libel, policy); book discusses tendencies and cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest, pathos, and delicacy of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Handling emotional material requires delicacy; human interest should not be exploited crudely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pathos judiciously; avoid sensational or tasteless details in deaths, funerals, and personal tragedies; be sensitive in wording and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature stories — planning and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Features require development of human interest, interviews, and narrative techniques distinct from daily hard news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect statistics, interviews, anecdotes; choose openings, play up features, use proportion and unity; many exercises suggest feature topics and approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of leads for specialized stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Different story types (accident, crime, sports, interviews, speeches, society, correspondence) demand different lead forms and emphases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to chapters on interviews, crime, sports, society, follow-ups, and correspondence for sample leads and treatment; tailor lead to the type and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines — accuracy and fit with copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines must accurately reflect the story and conform to the paper's style and length constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy readers write headlines after revising stories; headlines must avoid exaggeration and libel, fit length/space, and be slugged properly for compositors; bank-men and slugging practices are explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slugging, takes, and copy handling for production
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper slugging, cutting into takes, and using slugs/slug names are essential for efficient mechanical composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy cutter clips headlines, cuts copy into 'takes', marks slug names (catch lines) for bank-men/compositors; understanding linotype, galley proofs, stereotyping, and press-room timing helps the reporter meet deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading and marks used in correcting copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs are corrected systematically; the head proofreader and assistants detect typographical and factual errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three galley proofs go to managing editor, news editor, and head proofreader; corrected galley proof format and proofreader's marks are provided (specimen proof sheet and marks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/production awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should understand composing, stereotyping, and press-room processes to work within production constraints and exploit speed devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know linotype and monotype machines, bank-men, galley proofs, chutes, the 'fudge' for late news, and how news timing affects edition planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the morgue/library and exchange material
rubrics_metrics.description: The morgue provides background, obituaries, past accounts, and reference material to support quick story preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exchange editor supplies clippings; reporters use the morgue for historical context, boxed summaries, and rapid background when big news breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats and specialization (labor, marine, market, sporting, society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters often work assigned beats and should master the subject-matter, sources, and conventions of their beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the rhythms and rules of your beat (e.g., sporting editor must know rules and records instantly); cultivate contacts and correspondents; keep specialist space books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistics, figures, and government publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate and intelligible use of numbers and official sources enhances credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check figures, explain units and significance, use government publications and records where appropriate; chapter references include figures and filing dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding exaggeration and maintaining proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sensational overstatement; maintain proportion in emphasis and length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understatement can be valuable; do not overplay incidental facts; match tone and length to the story's true importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and style appropriate to purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Select tone (serious, humorous, informal) appropriate to story type, audience, and paper's style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to the paper's tone as determined by city/news editor; adapt to editors' preferences; maintain unity of impression and avoid inconsistent tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone and telegraph use / filing dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: Use telephone and telegraph effectively for gathering and filing news; handle telegraph copy and filing protocols properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know when to call, how to file dispatches, and the role of the telegraph editor; use special lines for speed; observe conventions for telegraph copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation, copy format, and mechanical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow prescribed copy format: margins, paragraph marks, marginal notes, end-marks, and use of longhand/typewriter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep clear margins, indicate paragraph indention, use end-mark and insert marks; submit neat copy to compositors and proofreaders; follow style book conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding ambiguity (pronouns, relation words, vagueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent ambiguity by clear antecedents for pronouns and precise relational phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch agreement of pronouns and verbs; avoid vague 'relation words' and ambiguous structures; clarity is repeatedly emphasized in sentence and paragraph guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrations and photographs when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and use visuals to support and enhance stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographers and cartoonists supply cuts; coordinate picture selection with city editor; use morgue photographs for background and prompt illustration of breaking news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical courtesy, dress, and demeanor
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should observe courtesy, appropriate dress, and conduct in interviews and the city room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be polite with sources, editors, and colleagues; adapt to city editor's preferences; use discretion in delicate assignments (society notes, personal columns).
